passage:
Sunday: Deepika sat with Tanuja on the balcony and wrote three questions in her notebook. Worst case? She'd lose the savings she had set aside for a stove and containers. Could she survive that? Yes, with her part-time job still paying the rent. Likely gain? Enough orders from the office blocks nearby to leave the job within a year.
Wednesday: Instead of quitting, she asked her manager for three days a week. She cooked lunch boxes for twelve people from Tanuja's office, as a trial.
Three weeks later: Twenty-six regular orders. Two complaints about salt, which she fixed. Her savings were still mostly there. 'Not rich,' she told Tanuja, 'but not frozen either.' She kept her back-up, the three days a week, for six more months.

qa.q: How many regular orders did Deepika have three weeks later?
qa.a: Twenty-six regular orders.

qa.q: What did Deepika mean by 'Not rich, but not frozen either'?
qa.a: She meant the lunch-box business wasn't making her rich yet, but she was glad she had acted instead of staying stuck.

qa.q: Which choice on Wednesday made the risk survivable?
qa.a: Asking for three days a week instead of quitting kept the rent covered while she tested lunch boxes with Tanuja's office.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see Deepika's careful questions on the balcony?
qa.a: Tanuja may see them as a steady way to try something bold without being reckless, and feel good about helping find the first twelve customers.

grounding: Shows a young adult weighing the worst outcome, whether it can be survived and the likely gain, then taking a step with a back-up plan.

passage:
Vidya, beta, you ask how your Nani opened the tailoring shop? Everyone in the mohalla called it Sarita's shop for thirty-one years, but at the start I was twenty-five, same as you. Your grandfather thought I'd lose everything, and he said so every night.
I sat with a slate and asked myself three things. What's the worst that can happen? I lose my gold bangles, which I had pawned to rent the room. Can I live through that? Yes, I still had my hands and the sewing work at home. What might I gain? A shop with my name, and enough to put your mother in a proper school.
So I didn't jump blind. I kept my old customers at home for the first year, just in case. I took the risk, but I kept a ladder behind me.
The shop lasted. Not because I was brave. Because I counted both sides.

qa.q: What had Sarita pawned to rent the room?
qa.a: Her gold bangles.

qa.q: What did Sarita believe made the shop last?
qa.a: She believed it lasted not because she was brave but because she counted both sides before acting.

qa.q: What choice kept Sarita's risk from being reckless?
qa.a: She kept her old customers at home for the first year, a ladder behind her in case the shop failed.

qa.q: How might hearing this story help Vidya with a risky choice now?
qa.a: Vidya might see that a big step can be taken carefully, by asking about the worst case and keeping a back-up, rather than being reckless or frozen.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how she weighed the worst outcome, its survivability and the likely gain, then took a step with a back-up plan.

passage: The offer to join Gurleen's small design studio expired in forty-eight hours, and Arohi's stable job came with a bonus she'd lose if she left before March. She sat on the floor of her Pune flat with a notebook and three questions. Worst outcome? The studio folds in a year and she's job-hunting. Could she survive it? Yes, with her savings and a strong portfolio. Likely gain? Real design work instead of the same brochures forever. She called her father, then an older colleague who had made a similar jump. Then she wrote a back-up plan: keep her old manager's goodwill, freelance at weekends if needed. At hour forty-six she emailed Gurleen: "Yes. Starting in April."

qa.q: How long did Arohi have before the offer expired?
qa.a: Forty-eight hours.

qa.q: How did Arohi seem to feel as she worked through the questions?
qa.a: She seemed calm and focused, not frozen or reckless, weighing both sides.

qa.q: Which steps made Arohi's choice a calculated risk?
qa.a: Asking the worst case, whether she could survive it and the likely gain, getting advice, and writing a back-up plan.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel reading "Yes. Starting in April"?
qa.a: Gurleen would likely feel delighted and relieved to have Arohi join.

grounding: Shows a young professional asking the worst case, whether it's survivable and the likely gain, then stepping forward with a back-up plan.

passage: Jatin had been offered a transfer to the Guwahati branch: a better role, a new city, no friends there. His sister Arohi found him at the dining table of their Chennai flat, making a list. "Worst case?" he read aloud. "I hate it, I'm lonely, I come back in a year." "Survivable?" she asked. "Yes. The company lets you apply back after twelve months." "Best likely case?" "I lead my own team. I learn Assamese. I see mountains." Arohi grinned. "And plan B?" He tapped the page: keep his room in the flat share for three months, a weekend call with old friends, a list of Chennai openings saved. He wasn't reckless. He wasn't frozen either. He signed the transfer letter.

qa.q: Where was Jatin's transfer to?
qa.a: The Guwahati branch.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel as he worked through the list?
qa.a: He felt steady and clear, neither reckless nor frozen.

qa.q: What did Jatin's list include that made the risk sensible?
qa.a: The worst case, whether it was survivable, the likely gain, and a plan B.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel about her brother leaving?
qa.a: Arohi seems supportive and proud, though she may miss him.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional weighing worst case, survivability and gain, then taking a step with a back-up plan.

passage:
"You're really leaving the bank to prepare full-time, Madhav?"
"Not leaving. Taking a year's unpaid leave, Rajni. I asked HR; they allow it."
"And if you don't clear the exam?"
"I've thought about that. Worst case: I go back to the same desk, a year behind my batch. Painful, not fatal."
"And money?"
"I've talked it through with a financial adviser, and my parents know the plan. I'll tutor two evenings a week."
Rajni sipped her tea. "Best case?"
"I get the job I've wanted since school."
"You sound calm."
"I'm scared too. But staying at the bank forever because I'm scared has a cost too."
She clinked her cup against his. "Then go."

qa.q: How long is Madhav's unpaid leave?
qa.a: A year.

qa.q: How does Madhav feel about the plan?
qa.a: He feels calm but also scared, accepting both.

qa.q: What makes Madhav's choice a calculated risk rather than a reckless one?
qa.a: He checked the worst case, took advice from a financial adviser, told his parents and kept a way back to his desk.

qa.q: How does Rajni respond once she hears the plan?
qa.a: Rajni seems reassured and supportive, clinking cups and telling him to go.

grounding: Shows a young adult treating a career risk as a choice with costs on both sides, with a back-up plan and proper advice.

passage:
Last spring I got into a six-month design residency in Lisbon. My first reaction was panic: I'll lose my job, I'll come back with nothing.
Tanvir made me sit down with a notebook. Three questions. What's the worst that can happen? That I come back and need to look for work for a few months. Could I survive that? Yes; I've done it before. What's the likely gain? A portfolio I couldn't build here, and people I'd never meet otherwise.
Then the back-up plan. I asked my manager about unpaid leave. She said no, but offered to write me a strong reference. I reached out to two former clients who said they'd send freelance work.
So I went. The residency was hard and wonderful. When I came back, it took me seven weeks to find a new role. Scary weeks, but survivable ones, exactly as I'd planned.
Eshaan

qa.q: How long was the design residency?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel on first getting into the residency?
qa.a: Eshaan felt panic, afraid of losing the job and coming back with nothing.

qa.q: How did Eshaan turn the choice into a calculated risk?
qa.a: By asking about the worst outcome, whether it was survivable and the likely gain, then setting up a back-up with a reference and freelance clients.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt watching Eshaan panic at first?
qa.a: Tanvir was probably concerned but steady, helping Eshaan think it through with three questions instead of deciding for Eshaan.

grounding: Shows a young adult weighing worst case, survivability and gain, then taking a residency with a back-up plan, neither reckless nor frozen.
